title: Is Canned Tuna Healthy? What to Know Before You Buy a Can
meta_description: Is canned tuna healthy? What a can gives you, how mercury differs between light and albacore, how to spot the sodium, and how to choose a can in 30 seconds.
excerpt: Canned tuna can be a healthy everyday fish. Here's what it gives you, how light and albacore differ on mercury, and how to read the sodium on the label.
author: sarah
content:
Canned tuna is the fish most of us grew up on. It's cheap, it keeps for years, and it turns into lunch in two minutes. So when you start eating more fish for your heart, it's fair to wonder whether that can counts, or whether mercury and salt mean you should skip it.

Here's the short answer: yes, canned tuna can be a healthy, everyday food, as long as you pick the right kind of tuna and read the sodium line on the label. If you'd like to see where your own calorie and protein numbers land before you plan meals around it, the free PescoDial calculator gives you a starting point based on your age, height and weight.

What a Can of Tuna Gives You

Let me explain why tuna earns its spot in the pantry. It's mostly protein with very little fat, and it has no carbohydrate at all. According to USDA FoodData Central, a 3-ounce serving of canned light tuna packed in water, drained, has about 17 grams of protein for roughly 75 calories. That's why it shows up in so many weight-loss lunches.

It also brings a few nutrients that matter more as we get older:

  • Vitamin B12. A 3-ounce serving has about 2.2 micrograms, roughly 90 percent of the 2.4 micrograms adults need each day. The NIH notes that many older adults make less stomach acid and absorb less of the B12 in food, so good food sources help.
  • Selenium. One serving has about 60 micrograms, a little more than the 55 micrograms adults need in a day.

The honest part about omega-3s

This is where canned tuna gets oversold. Light tuna is a lean fish, so it carries far less of the EPA and DHA your heart research talks about than the fatty fish do. A 3-ounce serving of canned light tuna has roughly 0.2 grams of EPA plus DHA. Canned albacore in water has more, about 0.7 grams. Canned sardines in oil come in around 0.8 grams, and canned pink salmon about 0.9 grams.

So think of light tuna as your lean-protein fish meal, not your heart-fat fish meal. It's a good food, just not a stand-in for salmon or sardines. I go through the fatty fish properly in which fish are actually high in omega-3.

Mercury: The Type of Tuna Decides It

All tuna is not the same fish. "Tuna" on a label can mean several species, and they sit in very different places on the FDA and EPA fish chart. Here's how they compare, using the FDA's measured averages:

What the label saysUsual speciesAverage mercury (ppm)FDA/EPA group
Chunk light, light, skipjackSkipjack0.126 (canned light)Best Choice
Solid white, white, albacoreAlbacore0.350 (canned albacore)Good Choice
Yellowfin (some steaks, some pouches, some "ahi")Yellowfin0.354 (fresh/frozen)Good Choice
Bigeye (steaks, sushi, some "ahi")Bigeye0.689 (fresh/frozen)Choice to Avoid

Two takeaways. Canned light tuna is in the lowest-mercury group, the same Best Choices list as salmon, sardines and shrimp. Canned albacore averages close to three times the mercury of canned light tuna in the FDA's testing, which is why it sits one group higher. It's still a reasonable fish, but the FDA and EPA chart suggests 1 serving a week from the Good Choices group.

Bigeye is on the FDA's list to avoid, so it isn't a tuna to eat. You won't usually find it in a can, but it does show up as tuna steaks and at sushi counters. If a menu just says "ahi" and nobody can tell you which tuna it is, choose a different dish.

One note on labels: the FDA lists canned light tuna, which includes skipjack, as a Best Choice. Brands that say "skipjack" on the label take out the guesswork.

Sodium: The Part Most People Miss

For a lot of readers, salt is the bigger everyday issue with canned tuna, not mercury. USDA FoodData Central lists regular canned light tuna in water at about 210 mg of sodium per 3-ounce serving, and canned albacore in water at about 320 mg. The no-salt-added version of light tuna comes in around 40 mg. That's a big difference from a single swap on the shelf.

And the tuna is rarely the end of it. Mayonnaise, pickles, crackers and bread all add their own sodium, so a tuna sandwich can carry far more salt than the can alone. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030, say adults should keep the whole day under 2,300 mg of sodium.

If you take medicine: canned tuna is a food choice, but a few medicines are worth a quick conversation. If you take blood-pressure medicine, the sodium in canned fish, and in what you mix it with, is the part to ask about. If you're on a blood thinner such as warfarin, take questions about eating more fish to your pharmacist, who knows your full medicine list. If you take diabetes medicine, a change in what's on your plate can change how your blood sugar runs. If you take a statin, your doctor or pharmacist can tell you whether a change in how you eat matters for you. Check with them before you change anything. This is not for everyone. Talk to your doctor first if you have high blood pressure, kidney or heart problems, diabetes, are pregnant, or take medicine.

Water or oil?

Water-packed tuna is the lighter choice. Oil-packed light tuna, drained, has noticeably more calories, roughly 170 per 3 ounces against about 75 for water-packed, based on USDA figures. Tuna in olive oil suits a Mediterranean-style plate, with the oil doubling as dressing. Check sodium either way, because the packing liquid doesn't decide the salt.

What about BPA in the can?

BPA is a chemical that has been used in some metal can coatings, and the FDA notes that small amounts of packaging materials can move into food. The FDA's current position is that BPA is safe at the levels found in food. If you'd still rather limit it, look for cans labeled BPA-free, or try tuna in pouches.

How to Choose a Can in 30 Seconds

When I do my mom's groceries on Wednesdays, the canned aisle is where she slows down and squints at labels, so we've made a routine of it:

  1. Look for "light" or "skipjack." That's the Best Choice. "Solid white" or "albacore" is fine once a week.
  2. Find the sodium line on the Nutrition Facts panel. Compare cans per serving. "No salt added" on the front makes it easy.
  3. Pick water or olive oil based on your calories and taste.
  4. Skip anything sold as bigeye, and pass on tuna steaks labeled only "ahi" unless you know the species.

How Often Does Canned Tuna Fit?

The FDA and EPA chart was written for people who are or may become pregnant and for young children. It suggests 2 to 3 servings a week from Best Choices, or 1 a week from Good Choices, and the same groups make a simple shopping guide for the rest of us. The FDA also points to the Dietary Guidelines advice of at least 8 ounces of seafood a week for adults on a 2,000-calorie diet. Canned light tuna can be one of those servings, with albacore held to once a week. The bigger question of how many servings to aim for, and how mercury fits into that, is covered in how much fish per week after 60.

Easy ways to eat it: tuna with olive oil, lemon, white beans and parsley, or tuna salad made with Greek yogurt in place of some of the mayo.

When to Talk to Your Doctor

Canned light tuna is on the FDA's lowest-mercury list. Still, get checked if you notice any of these:

  • New numbness, tingling or pins and needles in your hands, feet or around your mouth
  • New trouble with balance, walking or fine movements like buttoning a shirt
  • Home blood pressure readings that keep running above the target your doctor gave you
  • New swelling in your ankles or legs, or sudden weight gain over a few days
  • Unusual bruising, nosebleeds or bleeding gums if you take a blood thinner

Swelling of the lips or throat, hives or trouble breathing after eating fish is an emergency. Call 911 or your local emergency number.

The Bottom Line

Canned tuna is healthy for most people. Choose light or skipjack for everyday use, keep albacore to once a week, never buy bigeye, and read the sodium line before the can goes in your cart. Treat it as lean, affordable protein, and let salmon and sardines carry the omega-3s.
